Title: Caring for children with cleft lips and palate

content.text: Left lip and palate is the most common birth defect of the head and neck area. It is particularly common in Pakistan given the generally poor level of ante-natal care and the high rate of first cousin marriages," said Dr Tahir Shafi Khan, Assistant Professor and Consultant Plastic Surgeon at the Aga Khan University Hospital (AKUH). He was giving the presentation on "Team Approach to care for Children with Cleft lip and Palate" at 'Signs, Symptoms and Care' a monthly health awareness programme held on November 25, 2000.

Dr Tahir Shafi elaborated,"The condition can cause a severe physical deformity of the face. Due to the deformity there can be problems in feeding, speech, hearing, taste and smell as well as the normal development of the teeth and central part of the face. Moreover a significant number of these children have other birth defects in addition to cleft lip and palate. The presence of a cleft can be devastating for the child and family."

Dr Tahir Shafi said,"Comprehensive care of the child and family is usually necessary from birth to adulthood. A variety of health professionals are involved in providing this care in a coordinated sequence to best match the needs of the child at various stage of development. Recognizing this fact, medical centers all over the world, have organized multi-disciplinary cleft palate teams to provide optimum care to these children and their families."

Dr Tahir Shafi stressed,"It is the responsibility of the health care providers and the parents to realize that the treatment does not end with one or more operations but that follow up with the cleft palate team is required right up to adulthood. Teams of foreign doctors, comprising mainly of doctors in training, that fly in, operate 'conveyor belt-style' on these children and fly off again do not necessarily provide a service. These doctors practice on unknowing patients to whom they are not responsible or liable. No proper follow up is arranged for complications or ongoing, treatment. The above scenario could be condoned in the past due to the lack of sufficient plastic surgeons in the country."

"However, there are now approximately 50 plastic surgeons in the Pakistan Association of Plastic Surgeons and this body has been in existence for 5 years. There are members of this association in each of the major cities of Pakistan and the majority is attempting to apply the team approach to cleft lip and palate care. Given appropriate support and care children with this condition can be restored to a state of normality or near normality and it behoove all of us to strive for that goal,"stated Dr Tahir Shafi.

Another speaker, Dr Mehnaz Atiq, Assistant Professor and Consultant Pediatrician cardiologist at AKUH, explained,"Oral clefts (cleft lip and/or palate) are important congenital malformations that can severely compromise growth of infants. The risk factors associated with the poly-factorial disease have been identified to some extent. Important ones include consanguinity (akin), maternal illness, maternal drug intake and family history of congenital (birth) defects."

She further added,"The infants are usually troubled by difficulty in feeding milk, can aspirate milk, develop recurrent ear and lung infection, all this reflects as poor weight gain. There may be associated defects congenital in origins which probably have the same cause as clefts; these have to be looked for, sometimes through special investigations."
"Management issues are not easy and proper management in early infancy leads to a good outcome,"said Dr Mehnaz Atiq.
The panel, which consisted of Dr Mubashir Ikram and the speakers, answered questions for the audience at the end of the program.
